content.title: Power Series Intervals and Error
content.overview: This lesson focuses on determining the set of x-values for which a power series converges and quantifying the maximum possible error when using a Taylor polynomial to approximate a function.
learning_objectives: Calculate the radius and interval of convergence for a power series using the Ratio Test.
Test for convergence at the endpoints of the interval of convergence.
Apply the Lagrange Error Bound to determine the maximum possible error of a Taylor polynomial approximation.

sections.title: Radius and Interval of Convergence
sections.content:
A power series centered at c has the form Σ a_n(x - c)^n. To find the interval of convergence, we typically apply the Ratio Test to the absolute value of the terms. If the limit of |a_{n+1}(x-c)^{n+1} / a_n(x-c)^n| as n approaches infinity is L, the series converges when L < 1. This inequality is solved to find the radius of convergence (R). The series converges absolutely for |x - c| < R, meaning the open interval (c - R, c + R). The series diverges for |x - c| > R.

![A flow chart showing the steps: 1. Apply Ratio Test, 2. Solve for |x-c| < R, 3. Identify open interval, 4. Test endpoints individually, 5. State final interval.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/326e048f-39b3-4278-aac0-d00ac5f99058-1786526334953-686.webp)

sections.title: Endpoint Analysis
sections.content: The Ratio Test is inconclusive when L = 1, which occurs at the endpoints x = c - R and x = c + R. To determine the full interval of convergence, you must substitute these specific x-values back into the original power series and test the resulting numerical series for convergence using other tests, such as the p-series test, alternating series test, or integral test.

sections.title: Lagrange Error Bound
sections.content: When a function f(x) is approximated by its nth-degree Taylor polynomial P_n(x) centered at c, the remainder R_n(x) = f(x) - P_n(x) represents the error. The Lagrange Error Bound states that |R_n(x)| ≤ [M / (n+1)!] * |x - c|^(n+1), where M is the maximum value of the absolute value of the (n+1)th derivative of f on the interval between c and x. This provides a 'worst-case scenario' for the approximation error.

worked_examples.question: Find the interval of convergence for the power series Σ [ (x - 7)^n / (n * 3^n) ] from n=1 to infinity.
worked_examples.solution:
1. Apply Ratio Test: lim |[(x-7)^{n+1} / ((n+1)3^{n+1})] * [(n 3^n) / (x-7)^n]| = |x-7|/3 * lim |n/(n+1)| = |x-7|/3.
2. Set |x-7|/3 < 1, so |x-7| < 3. The radius R = 3. The open interval is (4, 10).
3. Test x = 4: Σ [ (4-7)^n / (n 3^n) ] = Σ [ (-3)^n / (n 3^n) ] = Σ [ (-1)^n / n ]. This is the alternating harmonic series, which converges.
4. Test x = 10: Σ [ (10-7)^n / (n 3^n) ] = Σ [ 3^n / (n 3^n) ] = Σ [ 1/n ]. This is the harmonic series, which diverges.
5. The interval of convergence is [4, 10).

worked_examples.question: Let f be a function such that |f'''(x)| ≤ 0.5 for all x in [2, 2.2]. Find the Lagrange error bound for the second-degree Taylor polynomial P_2(x) centered at c = 2 when approximating f(2.2).
worked_examples.solution:
1. Identify n: We are using P_2(x), so n = 2. The next derivative needed is n+1 = 3.
2. Identify M: The maximum of |f'''(x)| is given as 0.5.
3. Identify x and c: x = 2.2 and c = 2.
4. Apply formula: |R_2(2.2)| ≤ [0.5 / 3!] * |2.2 - 2|^3.
5. Calculate: |R_2(2.2)| ≤ [0.5 / 6] * (0.2)^3 = (1/12) * 0.008 = 0.008 / 12 ≈ 0.000667.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to test the endpoints of the interval of convergence.
Using the nth derivative instead of the (n+1)th derivative in the Lagrange Error Bound formula.
Confusing the radius of convergence (a distance) with the interval of convergence (a set of values).
Failing to use absolute values when setting up the Ratio Test.
exam_tips: If the Ratio Test limit is 0, the radius is infinity and the interval is (-∞, ∞).
If the Ratio Test limit is infinity (unless x=c), the radius is 0 and the series converges only at x=c.
In Lagrange Error problems, if the (n+1)th derivative is monotonic, check the endpoints of the interval [c, x] to find the maximum value M.
content.recap: The interval of convergence is found using the Ratio Test followed by individual endpoint analysis. The Lagrange Error Bound provides a numerical limit on the approximation error of a Taylor polynomial based on the maximum value of the next available derivative.

knowledge_claims.content: To find the radius of convergence for a power series, apply the Ratio Test to the general term and solve the inequality where the limit is less than 1.
The radius of convergence R is the distance from the center c to the edge of the interval where the power series converges.
A power series always converges at its center c, regardless of the radius of convergence.
The Ratio Test is inconclusive at the endpoints of the interval of convergence, requiring separate testing using other convergence tests.
The Lagrange Error Bound for an nth-degree Taylor polynomial is given by |R_n(x)| ≤ [max|f^(n+1)(z)| / (n+1)!] * |x - c|^(n+1) for z between c and x.
If the limit of the Ratio Test is 0 for all x, the radius of convergence is infinity and the interval of convergence is all real numbers.
If the limit of the Ratio Test is infinite for all x ≠ c, the radius of convergence is 0.
It is a mistake to assume a power series converges at an endpoint without testing it, even if the series converges on the open interval.
The value M in the Lagrange Error Bound represents an upper bound on the absolute value of the (n+1)th derivative on the interval [c, x].
Unlike the Alternating Series Error Bound, which uses the first omitted term, the Lagrange Error Bound uses the maximum value of the next derivative.
If a power series for f(x) has a radius of convergence R, the power series for f'(x) also has the same radius of convergence R.
When testing endpoints, if the substituted series is a p-series with p > 1, the series converges at that endpoint.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Power Series Intervals and Error — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Power Series Intervals and Error: A power series has a radius and endpoint-dependent interval of convergence, while Taylor remainder bounds quantify approximation error.
options.B: Basic Derivative Rules: Constant, power, sum, product, and quotient rules determine derivatives efficiently while preserving the structure of the original function.
options.C: Related Rates: Related-rates problems differentiate a constraint connecting changing quantities, then substitute simultaneous values and known rates.
options.D: Riemann Sums: Left, right, midpoint, and general Riemann sums approximate accumulated change by adding products of values and subinterval widths.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because A power series has a radius and endpoint-dependent interval of convergence, while Taylor remainder bounds quantify approximation error. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Power Series Intervals and Error — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Higher-Order Derivatives: Successive derivatives describe changing rates, such as velocity from position and acceleration from velocity, with units changing at each differentiation.
options.B: Power Series Intervals and Error: A power series has a radius and endpoint-dependent interval of convergence, while Taylor remainder bounds quantify approximation error.
options.C: Particle Motion: Position, velocity, speed, and acceleration are connected through derivatives, and direction changes occur when velocity changes sign.
options.D: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem: The Fundamental Theorem connects accumulation, antiderivatives, and net change and provides methods to evaluate definite integrals.
